quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, ~62 in 1880) may still be living; if so, his wife — Patrick's mother — would be named and her age recorded. If Thomas had died by 1880, Patrick (~35) might appear in his own household or with a widowed mother heading hers. Parents' birthplaces in this schedule would corroborate or potentially refine the Ireland-origin inference.

Collection 1325221 ('United States Census, 1900') is name-searchable. Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, ~55 in 1900, died March 1908) should appear. The 1900 schedule records birth month and year, parents' birth countries, marital status, and years married. Parents' birthplaces would corroborate the Ireland origin and potentially distinguish the county if a more specific entry was recorded. Years married and number of living children, if present, may lead to Patrick's wife and descendants who could carry oral knowledge of his parents.

A will naming Patrick as an heir would be direct evidence of the parent–child relationship; a surviving-spouse clause or an administration naming the widow would identify Patrick's mother.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: The 1880 US census is the first to record each person's relationship to the head of household explicitly. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, age ~62 in 1880) may still be alive; if Patrick Flynn (born ~1845, age ~35) appears in Thomas's household as 'son,' that relationship column supplies direct-relationship evidence unavailable from the 1850 or 1860 censuses. Even if Patrick had established his own separate household by 1880, his own census entry states his father's and mother's birthplaces, which are presently unknown. Searching both Thomas Flynn and Patrick Flynn in the United States Census, 1880 collection on FamilySearch, which is name-searchable, covers both angles. Variant spellings Flinn and Flyn should be tried. Prior plans pl_002 searched 1850 and 1860 only; no 1870 or 1880 census was searched for this question.

S4 ('Schuylkill County Probate Records') is already recorded in the project tree as a source description but carries no assertions. The locality guide (loc_001) confirms the Schuylkill County Register of Wills held probate from 1811 and is a primary parentage source: a will or administration naming Patrick Flynn as a son or heir would be direct evidence of the Thomas-Patrick relationship — stronger than any census inference or secondary death-certificate statement. Thomas Flynn born ~1818 could plausibly have died anywhere from the 1860s through ~1920; the date range is sized to his lifespan, not Patrick's. The Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 collection on FamilySearch is browse-only (personCount 0), requiring an image browse of the county's will books and administration dockets scoped to the Flynn surname.

If Thomas Flynn died on or after January 1906, a Pennsylvania state death certificate would exist in the Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 collection on FamilySearch, which is name-searchable. The informant on a parent's death certificate is typically a child of the deceased — making this a near-primary source for Thomas's parentage details in the next generation — and would also name Thomas's wife (Patrick's mother), who is presently unknown across all evidence gathered. If Thomas died before 1906, the substitute is the church burial records item in this plan. Thomas's lifespan (born ~1818) sets this item's date range at 1860-1920, not Patrick's research window. Variant spellings Flinn and Flyn should be tried.

A dedicated search for Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother is required for this parentage question. The marriage record: (a) establishes Thomas and his wife as a married couple before Patrick's birth ca. 1845; (b) supplies Patrick's mother's maiden name, which no census, death certificate, or other record in the project yet provides; and (c) corroborates Thomas as a father named so far only by indirect census co-residences and a secondary death-certificate statement from a son-in-law. Note the limit: the couple's marriage proves they married and dates their union but is not, by itself, evidence that Patrick is their child — a record placing Patrick with them is still needed. The Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 collection and Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 on FamilySearch are both name-searchable and should be searched. Thomas born ~1818 likely married ca. 1838-1855; the date range 1835-1865 covers that window plus possible later remarriage.

Patrick Flynn is listed as 'child_1' in the 1850 household and 'child_2' in the 1860 household of Thomas Flynn, indicating at least one sibling. Catholic baptism entries in Schuylkill County parish registers name both parents explicitly — father and mother — providing direct evidence linking Thomas Flynn and his wife to their children. A sibling's baptism naming 'Thomas Flynn and [wife]' as parents is direct parentage evidence for the whole sibling set, including Patrick. The locality guide (loc_001) confirms Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1961; sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records on FamilySearch is name-searchable. Patrick born ~1845 in Ireland per the tree's birth fact means his own baptism would be in an Irish parish, not here, but siblings born in Pennsylvania would appear in this collection. Search the Flynn surname with given names drawn from all household members visible in 1850 and 1860.

The 1870 census bridges the 10-year gap between the last confirmed household co-residence (1860) and the 1880 census. Thomas Flynn (~52) should appear in his own household; Patrick (~25) may still be there or may have established an adjacent or nearby household. A shared household or neighboring households in 1870 further establishes the family's continued presence in Schuylkill County and corroborates the chain of identity running through the 1850, 1860, 1880 censuses — an important link before asserting continuity relies on approximate age and surname alone. United States Census, 1870 on FamilySearch is name-searchable. Variant spellings Flinn and Flyn should be tried.

The 1900 census records each person's birth month and year, parents' birthplaces, years in the United States, and relationship to the head of household. Patrick Flynn (~55) would appear in his own household; the parents' birthplaces column would corroborate or extend what 1880 shows. Crucially, if Thomas Flynn's widow (Patrick's mother) were still alive and living with Patrick in 1900, she would appear by name in this record — the only surviving record type that would name her if Thomas's marriage record has not been found. United States Census, 1900 on FamilySearch is name-searchable.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

If Thomas Flynn (already in the tree as Patrick's father, I2, with no death year) is still alive, he may appear in Patrick's household or nearby. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records collection (name-searchable) covers Catholic and Protestant parishes from 1708-1985; per loc_001, Catholic parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia. The United States Civil War Soldiers Index (name-searchable) covers service records from which pension file references can be traced. Thomas Flynn born ~1818 was 43-47 — age for Pennsylvania home-guard or emergency militia service. Search both men. A pension record naming Thomas as Patrick's father would be direct parentage evidence independent of the death certificate.

Required FAN item for a parentage question. Thomas Flynn, born ~1818 in Ireland, would have needed to naturalize as a US citizen. The Schuylkill County Naturalization Records volume (007936750, 1849-1915) is browse-only (personCount 0). A Declaration of Intention or Petition for Naturalization names the declarant's age, birthplace, and arrival date — Thomas's Irish county of origin is the same origin Patrick inherits, which would resolve the birthplace conflict in ps_001 and identify the Irish parish for a future search. The witnesses to Thomas's naturalization were his contemporaneous FAN in the Pennsylvania Irish immigrant community; their names can be searched in census and probate records to find any document that mentions Patrick as a member of Thomas's family. A dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage is required on every parentage plan. Per Spanish naming conventions, the subject's father carried the first surname García and her mother the first surname Romero. The 'Spain, Marriages, 1565-1950' collection (name-searchable) covers this jurisdiction and period. The marriage record: (a) confirms the couple as a spousal unit; (b) supplies the mother's first/paternal surname (Romero — which may or may not be her birth surname if she previously married, though no prior marriage is known); (c) by date relative to the subject's birth about 1843, corroborates a parentage pair otherwise supported only by indirect evidence. Note the limit: the marriage record does not by itself place María Josefa as the couple's child — a record placing the child with the parents (her baptism or a padron entry) is still needed. Date window sized to when parents of a child born 1843 could plausibly have married, not the subject's own birth year.

The subject's own marriage record frequently names the bride's father and mother in this period, providing an independent statement of parentage separate from the baptism register. The 'Spain, Marriages, 1565-1950' collection (name-searchable) covers this jurisdiction and period. Born about 1843, María Josefa would likely have married between roughly 1858 and 1885; search under García Romero as a bride. A marriage entry naming both parents would corroborate or supplement findings from the baptism search.

Death and burial records often name the deceased's parents. Two sources apply: (1) church burial entries before 1871 — the 'Spain, Catholic Church Records, 1307-2005' collection (name-searchable) and image group 008216233_005 (Vélez-Málaga death records 1853-1861, full-text searchable but browse-only (personCount 0)); (2) civil registration death records from 1871 onward in the 'Spain, Deaths, 1600-1920' collection (name-searchable). Born about 1843, the subject's death most likely falls within this window. A death entry naming both parents would provide corroborating or independent parentage evidence. Date window sized to the collection's extent past the subject's birth window, since civil files assembled decades after the birth can testify to it.

A parentage question requires at least one FAN-cluster item. Siblings of María Josefa would have been baptized in the same Santa María parish under a García father and Romero mother. Finding a sibling's baptism entry naming the same parent pair corroborates the parentage identification independently of the subject's own entry, and may survive where the subject's entry is damaged or missing. Use the 'Spain, Baptisms, 1502-1940' collection (name-searchable), searching for children of a García father and Romero mother in Vélez-Málaga. Date range covers plausible sibling birth years (parents could have married by the early 1830s; siblings born across 1825-1862).

Spanish municipalities maintained periodic household registers (padrones de vecinos) recording all residents with relationships, ages and origins. The 'Spain, Málaga, Municipal Records, 1760-1956' collection (name-searchable) covers Vélez-Málaga and this period. A padron entry showing María Josefa listed as a child in a García/Romero household would be direct co-residence evidence placing her with candidate parents — complementing the baptism record and supplying a link between child and parents that neither a marriage record nor a baptism standing alone can provide.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

- Source SD-KER-1850: 1850 US Federal Census household of Patrick Kerrigan, 35, laborer, born Ireland; Mary, 32, born Ireland; **Thomas, 8, born Pennsylvania;** Pottsville, Schuylkill County.
- Proposed father: Patrick Kerrigan (ZZKR-PA4), born ~1815 County Mayo, Ireland; died 1880 Pottsville.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.
